title: V. The Grand Inquisitor
paragraphs: "Even this needs a preface—a literary one, I mean," Ivan laughed, "and I'm not much good at writing one. You see, my story takes place in the sixteenth century, and back then, as you probably learned in school, it was common in poetry to bring the powers of heaven down to earth. Never mind Dante—in France, clerks as well as monastery monks used to put on regular performances in which the Madonna, the saints, the angels, Christ, even God Himself, were brought onto the stage. In those days it was all done with perfect innocence. In Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris, an edifying, free spectacle was staged for the people at the Hôtel de Ville in Paris, during the reign of Louis XI, to celebrate the birth of the dauphin. It was called Le bon jugement de la très sainte et gracieuse Vierge Marie, and the Virgin herself appears on stage and delivers her bon jugement. Similar plays, mostly drawn from the Old Testament, were occasionally performed in Moscow too, right up through the reign of Peter the Great. But besides actual plays, there were all sorts of legends and ballads scattered across the world in which saints and angels and every power of Heaven took part whenever the story called for them. In our monasteries, the monks busied themselves translating, copying, even composing poems of that kind—even under the Tatars. There's one, for instance—from the Greek, of course—called The Wanderings of Our Lady Through Hell, with descriptions as bold as Dante's. Our Lady visits hell, and the Archangel Michael guides her through the torments. She sees the sinners and their punishments. Among them she notices one particularly striking group of sinners sunk in a burning lake; some of them sink so deep they can never swim back up, and 'these, God forgets'—a phrase of extraordinary depth and force. And so Our Lady, shaken and weeping, falls down before the throne of God and begs mercy for everyone in hell—for everyone she saw there, without exception. Her exchange with God is fascinating. She pleads, she won't let up, and when God points to the hands and feet of her Son, nailed to the Cross, and asks, 'How can I forgive His tormentors?', she calls on all the saints, all the martyrs, all the angels and archangels to fall down beside her and pray for mercy on everyone, without distinction. It ends with her winning a yearly reprieve from suffering, from Good Friday to Trinity Day, and the sinners in hell immediately cry out in gratitude, chanting: 'Thou art just, O Lord, in this judgment.' Well, my poem would have been something along those lines, if it had appeared back then. He appears on the scene in my poem, but He says nothing—He simply appears, and passes on. Fifteen centuries have gone by since He promised to come in His glory, fifteen centuries since His prophet wrote, 'Behold, I come quickly'; 'of that day and that hour knoweth no man, neither the Son, but the Father,' as He Himself foretold while on earth. But humanity still waits for Him with the same faith, the same love. Oh, with even greater faith, since it's been fifteen centuries since man stopped seeing signs from heaven."
No signs from heaven come today / To back up what the heart doth say.

"There was nothing left but faith in what the heart says. It's true, there were plenty of miracles in those days. There were saints who performed miraculous cures; some holy people, according to their biographies, were visited by the Queen of Heaven herself. But the devil never sleeps, and doubts about the truth of these miracles had already started creeping in among men. And right around then a terrifying new heresy sprang up in northern Germany. 'A huge star, like a torch'—meaning a church—'fell upon the sources of the waters, and they became bitter.' These heretics began blasphemously denying miracles outright. But those who stayed faithful believed all the more fervently for it. Humanity's tears rose up to Him as before, waiting for His coming, loving Him, hoping in Him, yearning to suffer and die for Him just as before. And after so many centuries of praying with faith and fervor, 'O Lord our God, hasten Thy coming,' after calling on Him for so many ages, He, in His infinite mercy, chose to come down among His servants once more. Before that day, He had come down before—He'd visited certain holy men, martyrs and hermits, as their lives record. Among us, Tyutchev, with absolute faith in the truth of what he wrote, testified that"
Bearing the Cross, in slavish dress, Weary and worn, the Heavenly King Our mother Russia came to bless, And through our land went wandering.
"And that certainly was so, I assure you.

"And behold, He chose to appear, if only for a moment, to His people—the tortured, suffering people, sunk in wickedness, yet loving Him like children. My story is set in Spain, in Seville, at the most terrible height of the Inquisition, when fires were lit every day to the glory of God, and 'in a splendid auto-da-fé the wicked heretics were burned.' Oh, of course this isn't the coming He promised, the one where He will appear at the end of time in the full glory of heaven, sudden 'as lightning flashing from east to west.' No, He came to visit His children only for a moment, right there where the flames were crackling around the heretics. In His infinite mercy He walked once more among men in that same human form in which He had walked among them for three years, fifteen centuries before. He came down onto the 'hot pavements' of that southern town, where only the day before, almost a hundred heretics had been burned, ad majorem gloriam Dei, by the cardinal, the Grand Inquisitor, in a magnificent auto-da-fé, before the king, the court, the knights, the cardinals, the loveliest ladies of the court, and the entire population of Seville."

"He came quietly, unnoticed, and yet, strange to say, everyone recognized Him. This might be one of the best parts of the poem—I mean, why they recognized Him. The people are irresistibly drawn to Him, they crowd around Him, gather close, follow Him. He moves silently among them with a gentle smile of infinite compassion. The sun of love burns in His heart, light and power pour from His eyes, and their radiance, falling on the people, stirs their hearts with an answering love. He holds out His hands to them, blesses them, and a healing power flows from His touch, even just from touching His clothes. An old man in the crowd, blind since childhood, cries out, 'O Lord, heal me, and I shall see Thee!' and something like scales fall from his eyes, and the blind man sees Him. The crowd weeps and kisses the earth beneath His feet. Children throw flowers before Him, sing, cry out hosanna. 'It is He—it is He!' they all repeat. 'It must be Him, it can be no one else!' He stops at the steps of Seville Cathedral just as weeping mourners are carrying in a small open white coffin. Inside lies a child of seven, the only daughter of a prominent citizen. The dead child lies buried in flowers. 'He will raise your child,' the crowd shouts to the weeping mother. The priest, coming out to meet the coffin, looks baffled and frowns, but the dead child's mother throws herself at His feet with a wail. 'If it is truly Thou, raise my child!' she cries, stretching her hands toward Him. The procession stops, the coffin is set down on the steps at His feet. He looks on with compassion, and His lips softly say once more: 'Maiden, arise.' And the maiden rises. The little girl sits up in the coffin and looks around, smiling with wide, wondering eyes, still holding the bunch of white roses they'd placed in her hand."

"There are cries, sobs, confusion among the crowd, and at that very moment the cardinal himself, the Grand Inquisitor, passes by the cathedral. He is an old man, almost ninety, tall and upright, with a withered face and sunken eyes in which a gleam of light still lingers. He isn't wearing his magnificent cardinal's robes, as he was the day before, when he was burning the enemies of the Roman Church—at this moment he wears his coarse, old monk's cassock. Following him, at some distance, come his grim assistants and slaves and the 'holy guard.' He stops at the sight of the crowd and watches from a distance. He sees everything; he sees them set the coffin down at His feet, sees the child rise, and his face darkens. He knits his thick gray brows, and his eyes flash with a sinister fire. He points a finger and orders the guards to seize Him. And such is his power, so completely have the people been cowed into trembling obedience to him, that the crowd immediately parts for the guards, and in dead silence they lay hands on Him and lead Him away. The crowd instantly bows to the ground, as one man, before the old Inquisitor. He blesses the people in silence and moves on. The guards lead their prisoner to the cramped, gloomy, vaulted prison inside the ancient palace of the Holy Inquisition, and lock Him in. The day passes, followed by the dark, scorching, 'breathless' night of Seville. The air 'smells of laurel and lemon.' In the pitch darkness, the iron door of the prison suddenly opens, and the Grand Inquisitor himself walks in, carrying a light. He is alone; the door closes behind him at once. He stands in the doorway and for a minute or two gazes into His face. At last he walks up slowly, sets the light down on the table, and speaks."

"'Is it Thou? Thou?' But getting no answer, he adds at once, 'Don't answer, stay silent. What could You possibly say, anyway? I already know full well what You would say. And You have no right to add a single word to what You said long ago. Then why have You come to get in our way? For You have come to get in our way, and You know it perfectly well. But do You know what will happen tomorrow? I don't know who You are, and I don't care to know whether it's really You, or only something in Your likeness, but tomorrow I will condemn You and burn You at the stake as the worst of heretics. And the very people who kissed Your feet today will, at the first sign from me, rush to pile the embers of Your fire even higher. Do You know that? Yes, perhaps You do know it,' he added, with a thoughtful, searching look, never once taking his eyes off the Prisoner."

"I don't quite follow, Ivan. What does it all mean?" Alyosha, who had been listening in silence, asked with a smile. "Is it just some wild fantasy, or is the old man making some kind of mistake—some impossible case of mistaken identity?"

"Take it as the last one, if you like," Ivan said, laughing, "if you're so corrupted by modern realism that you can't stomach anything fantastical. If you'd rather it be a case of mistaken identity, let it be that. It's true," he went on, laughing, "the old man was ninety, and he might well have gone half-mad clinging to his fixed idea. He might have simply been struck by the Prisoner's appearance. It might, in fact, be nothing more than the ravings of a ninety-year-old, overwrought by yesterday's auto-da-fé of a hundred heretics. But does it really matter to us whether it was mistaken identity or pure fantasy? All that matters is that the old man finally speaks his mind, speaks openly about what he's kept silent for ninety years."
"And the Prisoner is silent too? He just looks at him and doesn't say a word?"

"That's unavoidable, in any version of the story," Ivan laughed again. "The old man has already told Him He has no right to add anything to what He said long ago. You might say that's the most fundamental feature of Roman Catholicism—in my opinion, at least. 'Everything has been handed over by You to the Pope,' they say, 'and so everything now rests in the Pope's hands, and there's no need for You to come back at all. For now, at least, You mustn't interfere.' That's how they talk, and how they write too—the Jesuits, anyway. I've read it myself in the works of their theologians. 'Do You have the right to reveal to us even one of the mysteries of that world You came from?' my old man asks Him, and then answers the question for Him. 'No, You do not; because that would mean adding to what was said long ago, and would strip men of the freedom You exalted so highly while You walked the earth. Anything You reveal now, anything new, will encroach on men's freedom of belief, because it will present itself as a miracle, and the freedom of their faith was dearer to You than anything else, back then, fifteen hundred years ago. Didn't You say, often enough, in those days, "I will make you free"? But now You've seen these "free" men,' the old man adds suddenly, with a pensive smile. 'Yes, we've paid a heavy price for it,' he goes on, looking sternly at Him, 'but at last we've finished that work, in Your name. For fifteen centuries we have wrestled with Your freedom, but now it is finished, over for good. You don't believe it's over for good? You look at me so meekly, and don't even deign to be angry with me. But let me tell You: right now, today, people are more convinced than ever that they possess complete freedom, and yet they've brought that very freedom to us and laid it humbly at our feet. And that has been our doing. Is this what You wanted? Is this the freedom You meant?'"
"I don't follow again," Alyosha broke in. "Is he being ironic? Is he joking?"

"Not in the least! He claims it as an achievement, for himself and his Church, that at last they've conquered freedom, and done so in order to make men happy. 'For now'—he's talking about the Inquisition, of course—'for the first time, it's become possible to think about the happiness of men. Man was created a rebel; and how can rebels be happy?' he says to Him. 'You were warned. You had no shortage of admonitions and warnings, but You wouldn't heed them; You rejected the only way men could ever be made happy. But fortunately, on Your way out, You passed the work on to us. You promised it, You established it by Your own word, You gave us the right to bind and to loose, and now, of course, You can't possibly think of taking that back. So why have You come to get in our way now?'"
"And what does he mean by 'no shortage of admonitions and warnings'?" Alyosha asked.
"Why, that's the heart of what the old man has to say.

"'The wise and dread spirit, the spirit of self-destruction and non-existence,' the old man goes on, 'the great spirit spoke with You in the wilderness, and we're told in the books that he "tempted" You. Is that so? And could anything truer ever have been said than what he revealed to You in those three questions, which You rejected, and which the books call "the temptation"? And yet, if there has ever been a truly stupendous miracle on this earth, it happened that day, the day of the three temptations. The very posing of those three questions was itself the miracle. Suppose, just for the sake of argument, that those three questions from the dread spirit had vanished entirely from the books, and that we had to reconstruct them, invent them fresh, and to do so gathered together every wise man on earth—rulers, high priests, scholars, philosophers, poets—and set them the task of inventing three questions that would not only fit the occasion, but would express, in three words, three human phrases, the entire future history of the world and of humanity—do You believe that all the combined wisdom of the earth could have come up with anything to match, in depth and force, the three questions actually put to You then, by the wise and mighty spirit in the wilderness? From those three questions alone, from the sheer miracle of how they're framed, we can see that we're dealing here not with the fleeting intelligence of man, but with something absolute, something eternal. Because in those three questions, the entire subsequent history of mankind is, as it were, gathered together into one whole and foretold in advance, and in them are united every unresolved contradiction of human nature. At the time it couldn't have been so clear, since the future was still unknown; but now that fifteen hundred years have passed, we can see that everything in those three questions was so rightly foreseen, so precisely foretold, and has come true so exactly, that nothing can be added to them, and nothing taken away.

"'Judge for Yourself who was right—You, or the one who questioned You then? Remember the first question; its meaning, put another way, was this: "You want to go out into the world, and You're going empty-handed, carrying nothing but some promise of freedom that men, in their simplicity and their natural unruliness, can't even understand, a freedom they fear and dread—because nothing has ever been more unbearable for a man, or for human society, than freedom. But do You see these stones, here in this parched and barren wilderness? Turn them into bread, and mankind will run after You like a flock of sheep, grateful and obedient, though forever trembling for fear You might withdraw Your hand and take back Your bread." But You wouldn't strip man of his freedom, and You rejected the offer, thinking: what is that freedom worth, if obedience has to be bought with bread? You answered that man does not live by bread alone. But do You know that for the sake of that earthly bread, the spirit of the earth will rise up against You, will fight You and defeat You, and everyone will follow him, crying out, "Who can compare to this beast? He has given us fire from heaven!" Do You know that the ages will pass, and humanity will proclaim, through the mouths of its wise men, that there is no such thing as crime, and therefore no sin—only hunger? "Feed men first, and then ask virtue of them!"—that's what they'll write on the banner they raise against You, the very banner with which they'll tear down Your temple. Where Your temple stood, a new building will rise; the terrible Tower of Babel will be built all over again, and though, like the first one, it will never be finished, still, You could have prevented that new tower, could have spared men a thousand years of suffering; because after a thousand years of agony with their tower, they'll come back to us all the same. They will seek us out again, hidden underground in the catacombs, because we will be persecuted and tortured all over again. They will find us, and cry out to us: "Feed us, because those who promised us fire from heaven never gave it!" And then we will finish building their tower for them, because it is the one who feeds them who finishes the building. And we alone will feed them in Your name, falsely claiming it is done in Your name. Oh, never, never will they be able to feed themselves without us! No science will ever give them bread as long as they remain free. In the end they will lay their freedom at our feet and say to us, "Make us your slaves, but feed us." They will understand, at last, that freedom and bread enough for everyone can never coexist, because they will never, ever manage to share it fairly among themselves! They will become convinced, too, that they can never truly be free, because they are weak, corrupt, worthless, and rebellious. You promised them the bread of Heaven, but I say again, can that possibly compare, in the eyes of the weak, the eternally sinful, the ignoble race of man, to earthly bread? And if, for the sake of the bread of Heaven, thousands follow You, what becomes of the millions, the tens of thousands of millions of souls who won't have the strength to give up earthly bread for the sake of heavenly bread? Or do You only care about the tens of thousands of the great and the strong, while the millions, countless as the sands of the sea, who are weak but love You, exist only to serve the great and the strong? No—we care for the weak too. They are sinful and rebellious, but in the end they too will become obedient. They will marvel at us, look on us as gods, because we are willing to bear the very freedom they found so terrifying, and rule over them instead—so dreadful will it seem to them, to be free. But we will tell them that we are Your servants, ruling in Your name. We will deceive them once again, because we will never let You come to us again. That deception will be our own suffering, because we will be forced to lie.

"'This is the meaning of the first question in the wilderness, and this is what You rejected, all for the sake of that freedom which You valued above everything else. And yet hidden inside that question lies the great secret of this world. Choosing "bread," You would have satisfied the universal, everlasting craving of humanity—to find someone to worship. As long as man remains free, nothing torments him and drives him more relentlessly than the search for someone to worship. But man doesn't just want something he alone can worship—he wants something established beyond all dispute, something everyone could agree at once to worship together. Because these pitiful creatures aren't only concerned with finding something one person or another can worship—they need to find something all of them can believe in and worship together; what matters above all is that they be together in it. This craving for a shared act of worship is the deepest misery of every man individually, and of all humanity, since the beginning of time. For the sake of shared worship, they've slaughtered each other with the sword. They've set up gods and challenged one another: "Cast aside your gods and come worship ours, or we will kill you and your gods too!" And so it will go on until the end of the world, even once gods have vanished from the earth entirely—men will still bow down before idols all the same. You knew, You had to have known, this fundamental secret of human nature, and yet You rejected the one infallible banner that was offered You, the one that would have made every man bow down to You alone—the banner of earthly bread; and You rejected it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. And look at what You did next. And again, all in the name of freedom! I tell You, nothing torments a man more than the anxiety of finding someone, quickly, to whom he can hand over that gift of freedom the poor creature was born with. But only someone who can set his conscience at rest can take that freedom from him. In bread, an unbeatable banner was offered You: give bread, and man will worship You, because nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gains control of his conscience—oh, then he will throw away Your bread and follow whoever has captured his conscience instead. In that, You were right. Because the secret of human existence isn't merely to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm sense of what he's living for, a man won't consent to go on living at all, and would sooner destroy himself than stay on this earth, even surrounded by bread. That much is true. But what happened instead? Instead of taking men's freedom away from them, You made it greater than ever! Did You forget that man would rather have peace, even death, than freedom to choose between good and evil? Nothing seduces a man more than freedom of conscience, but nothing causes him greater suffering either. And look what You did: instead of giving men something solid to rest their conscience on forever, You chose everything that was exceptional, vague, and enigmatic; You chose things that lay entirely beyond human strength, acting as though You didn't love them at all—You, who came to give Your very life for them! Instead of taking hold of men's freedom, You expanded it, and burdened the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its agonies forever. You wanted man's free love, wanted him to follow You freely, drawn and captivated by You of his own will. In place of the old, rigid law, man would now have to decide for himself, freely, what is good and what is evil, with only Your image before him as a guide. But didn't You know that in the end he would reject even Your image, even Your truth, once he was crushed under the terrible weight of free choice? They will cry out at last that the truth isn't in You at all, because they could never have been left in greater confusion and suffering than what You caused them, burdening them with so many cares, so many unanswerable questions.

"'So that, in truth, it was You Yourself who laid the foundation for the destruction of Your own kingdom, and no one else bears more of the blame for it. And yet what was offered to You? There are three powers, only three, capable of conquering and holding forever captive the conscience of these weak rebels, for their own happiness—those forces are miracle, mystery, and authority. You rejected all three, and set the example for rejecting them. When the wise and dread spirit set You on the pinnacle of the temple and said to You, "If You want to know whether You are the Son of God, then cast Yourself down, for it is written: the angels shall bear Him up, lest He fall and hurt Himself, and then You will know whether You are truly the Son of God, and will prove then how great Your faith in Your Father is." But You refused, and would not cast Yourself down. Oh, of course, You acted with pride and with dignity, as befits God; but the weak, unruly race of men—are they gods? Oh, You knew even then that in taking one step, in making even one motion to throw Yourself down, You would be tempting God and would have lost all faith in Him, and would have been dashed to pieces on the very earth You came to save. And the wise spirit who tempted You would have rejoiced. But I ask again: are there many like You? Could You seriously believe, even for a moment, that men too could withstand a temptation like that? Is human nature really such that it can reject miracle, and at the great moments of life, the moments of its deepest, most agonizing spiritual struggle, cling only to the free verdict of the heart? Oh, You knew Your deed would be written into books, passed down through distant ages to the furthest ends of the earth, and You hoped that man, following Your example, would cling to God without demanding a miracle. But You didn't know that when man rejects miracle, he rejects God along with it; because man doesn't search so much for God as for the miraculous. And since man can't bear to live without the miraculous, he will go and invent new miracles of his own, and will worship deeds of sorcery and witchcraft, even if he's a rebel, a heretic, and an unbeliever a hundred times over. You didn't come down from the cross when they shouted up at You, mocking and jeering, "Come down from the cross and we will believe that it is You." You didn't come down, because once again You refused to enslave man through a miracle, and craved a faith freely given, not one built on miracle. You craved free love, not the base raptures of a slave forever cowering before a power that has crushed him into submission. But in that, You thought too highly of men, because they are slaves, of course, however rebellious by nature. Look around and judge for Yourself; fifteen centuries have passed—look at them now. Whom have You managed to raise up to Yourself? I swear, man is weaker and baser by nature than You ever believed him to be! Can he, can he possibly do what You did? By showing him so much respect, You stopped, in a sense, feeling for him at all, because You asked far too much of him—You, who loved him more than You loved Yourself! Had You respected him less, You would have asked less of him. That would have been closer to love, because his burden would have been lighter. He is weak and vile. What does it matter that he's now rebelling everywhere against our authority, proud of his own rebellion? It's the pride of a child, a schoolboy. They're small children, rioting, locking the teacher out of the classroom. But their childish glee will come to an end; it will cost them dearly. They will tear down temples and soak the earth in blood. But eventually they'll see, these foolish children, that although they are rebels, they are powerless rebels, unable even to sustain their own rebellion. Drowning in their own foolish tears, they will finally recognize that He who made them rebels must have meant to mock them. They will say this in despair, and the saying of it will be a blasphemy that will make them even more miserable still, because human nature cannot bear blasphemy, and always, in the end, avenges it on itself. And so unrest, confusion, and misery—that is man's present lot, after You bore so much for the sake of his freedom! The great prophet describes, in vision and image, seeing all those who took part in the first resurrection, twelve thousand from each tribe. But if there were that many of them, they couldn't have been men—they must have been gods. They had carried Your cross, endured decades in the barren, starving wilderness, living on locusts and roots—and You may indeed point to them with pride, these children of freedom, of free love, of free and glorious sacrifice made in Your name. But remember, there were only a few thousand of them; and what of the rest? How are the other weak ones to blame, for failing to endure what the strong endured? How is a weak soul to blame for being unable to receive such terrible gifts? Can it really be that You came only for the elect, and only to the elect? If so, then it is a mystery, and we cannot understand it. And if it is a mystery, then we too have the right to preach a mystery, and to teach men that what matters isn't the free judgment of their hearts, isn't love, but a mystery they must follow blindly, even against their own conscience. And that is exactly what we have done. We have corrected Your work, and have built it instead on miracle, mystery, and authority. And men rejoiced that they were once again being led like sheep, that the terrible gift which had caused them such suffering was finally lifted from their hearts. Were we right to teach them this? Speak! Did we not love mankind, in so meekly acknowledging their weakness, so lovingly lightening their burden, permitting their feeble nature even to sin, with our blessing? Why have You come now to stand in our way? And why do You look at me so silently, so searchingly, with those gentle eyes? Be angry instead. I don't want Your love, because I do not love You. And what use is there in hiding anything from You? Don't I know exactly who I'm speaking to? Everything I could possibly say, You already know. And is it my place to hide our mystery from You? Perhaps it is Your will to hear it from my own lips. Then listen. We are not working with You—we are working with him. That is our mystery. It has been eight long centuries since we sided with him instead of with You. Exactly eight centuries ago, we took from him what You rejected with such scorn—that last gift he offered You, showing You all the kingdoms of the earth. We took Rome and Caesar's sword from him, and declared ourselves the sole rulers of the earth, though we still haven't managed to complete our work. But whose fault is that? Oh, the work has only just begun, but it has begun. It still has a long way to go before it's finished, and the earth still has much to suffer, but we will triumph, and we will be Caesars, and then we will plan the universal happiness of man. But You, too, could have taken up Caesar's sword back then. Why did You reject that last gift? Had You accepted that last piece of counsel from the mighty spirit, You would have given man everything he seeks on earth—someone to worship, someone to hold his conscience for him, and some way to unite everyone into one unanimous, harmonious ant-heap, since the craving for universal unity is the third and final anguish of mankind. Humanity as a whole has always striven to organize itself into a universal state. There have been many great nations with great histories, but the more highly developed they became, the more unhappy they were, because they felt the craving for worldwide union more acutely than other peoples did. The great conquerors, the Tamerlanes and Genghis Khans, swept like hurricanes across the face of the earth, striving to subdue its peoples, and they too were nothing but the unconscious expression of that same craving for universal unity. Had You taken the world and Caesar's purple robe, You would have founded a universal state and given the world universal peace. Because who can rule men, if not the one who holds their conscience and their bread in his hands? We have taken up Caesar's sword, and in taking it, of course, we rejected You and followed him instead. Oh, ages still lie ahead, ages of the chaos of free thought, of their science, and of cannibalism. Because having begun building their Tower of Babel without us, they will end, inevitably, in cannibalism. But then the beast will come crawling to us, licking our feet, spattering them with bloody tears. And we will sit astride the beast and raise up the cup, and on it will be written: "Mystery." But only then, and not before, will the reign of peace and happiness come for men. You take pride in Your elect, but You have only the elect, while we bring rest to everyone. And besides, how many of those elect, those mighty ones who might have joined the elect, have grown weary of waiting for You, and have already, or will yet, transfer all the strength of their spirit and the warmth of their hearts to the other camp, and end up raising their own free banner against You. You Yourself raised that banner. But with us, everyone will be happy, and will never again rebel or destroy one another as they did under Your freedom. Oh, we will convince them that they will only become free once they renounce their freedom to us and submit to us. And will we be right, or will we be lying? They will be convinced we are right, because they will remember the horrors of slavery and chaos that Your freedom brought down on them. Freedom, free thought, and science will lead them into such dead ends, will bring them face to face with such wonders and unsolvable mysteries, that some of them—the fierce, the rebellious—will destroy themselves; others, rebellious but weak, will destroy one another; while the rest, weak and wretched, will crawl fawning to our feet and whimper to us: "Yes, you were right, you alone hold His mystery, and we are coming back to you—save us from ourselves!"

"'Receiving bread from our hands, they will see clearly enough that we're only taking the bread their own hands made and giving it back to them, with no miracle involved at all. They will see that we don't turn stones into bread—but in truth, they will be far more grateful for receiving it from our hands than for the bread itself! Because they will remember only too well how, in the old days, without our help, even the bread they made with their own hands turned to stones in those hands, while ever since they came back to us, even the stones themselves have turned to bread in their hands. They will know, only too well, the value of complete submission! And until men understand that, they will remain unhappy. Who is most to blame for their not understanding it—speak! Who scattered the flock and sent it wandering down unknown paths? But the flock will gather together again, and will submit once more, and this time it will be for good. Then we will give them the quiet, humble happiness of the weak little creatures they are by nature. Oh, we will finally persuade them not to be proud, because it was You who lifted them up and thereby taught them pride in the first place. We will show them that they are weak, that they are nothing but pitiful children—but that a child's happiness is the sweetest of all. They will grow timid, will look to us, will huddle close to us in fear, like chicks to a hen. They will marvel at us, stand in awe of us, and take pride in the fact that we are so powerful and so clever that we've managed to subdue such a turbulent flock of thousands upon millions. They will tremble helplessly at our anger, their minds will grow fearful, they will be as quick to tears as women and children—but just as ready, at a single sign from us, to burst into laughter and rejoicing, into happy mirth and childish song. Yes, we will put them to work, but in their hours of leisure we will turn their lives into a child's game, complete with children's songs and innocent dances. Oh, we will even let them sin—they are weak and helpless, after all, and they will love us like children precisely because we let them sin. We will tell them that every sin will be forgiven, so long as it's committed with our permission; that we allow them to sin because we love them, and that we ourselves will bear the punishment for those sins. And we will bear it, and they will adore us as their saviors, who have taken their sins upon themselves before God. And they will keep no secrets from us. We will permit or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, to have children or not—depending on whether they've been obedient or disobedient—and they will submit to us gladly, cheerfully. Even the most painful secrets of their conscience, all of them, they will bring to us, and we will have an answer for every one. And they will be glad to believe our answer, because it will spare them the great anxiety and terrible agony they currently endure whenever they have to make a free decision for themselves. And everyone will be happy, all the millions upon millions of creatures, except for the hundred thousand who rule over them. Because only we, we who guard the mystery, will be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy infants, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken upon themselves the curse of knowing good and evil. They will die peacefully, they will pass away peacefully in Your name, and beyond the grave they will find nothing at all but death. But we will keep the secret, and for the sake of their happiness, we will lure them on with the promise of a heavenly, eternal reward. Though if there really were anything waiting in the next world, it certainly wouldn't be meant for the likes of them. It is foretold that You will come again in victory, that You will come with Your chosen ones, the proud and the strong—but we will say that they have only saved themselves, while we have saved everyone. We are told that the harlot who sits upon the beast, holding the mystery in her hands, will be put to shame, that the weak will rise up again and tear off her royal purple robe and strip bare her loathsome body. But then I will stand up and point out to You the thousand million happy children who have never known sin. And we, who took their sins upon ourselves for the sake of their happiness, will stand before You and say: "Judge us if You can, and if You dare." Know this: I do not fear You. Know that I too was in the wilderness, that I too lived on roots and locusts, that I too prized the freedom with which You blessed mankind, and that I too once strove to stand among Your elect, among the strong and the powerful, longing "to make up the number." But I woke up, and refused to serve madness. I turned back and joined the ranks of those who have corrected Your work. I left the proud behind and went back to the humble, for the sake of the happiness of the humble. What I am telling You will come to pass, and our dominion will be built. I tell You again: tomorrow You will see that obedient flock, who at a single sign from me will rush to pile the burning coals high around the stake where I will burn You for daring to stand in our way. Because if anyone has ever deserved our fires, it is You. Tomorrow I will burn You. Dixi.'"
Ivan stopped. He'd gotten carried away while talking, speaking with real excitement; but once he'd finished, he suddenly smiled.
Alyosha had listened in silence; toward the end he'd grown deeply moved, and had seemed several times on the verge of interrupting, but had held himself back. Now his words came out in a rush.

"But... that's absurd!" he cried, flushing. "Your poem is praise for Jesus, not condemnation of Him—the opposite of what you meant it to be. And who's going to believe you about freedom? Is that really how it's meant to be understood? That's not what the Orthodox Church teaches at all.... That's Rome, and not even the whole of Rome—it's a distortion—it's the worst of the Catholics, the Inquisitors, the Jesuits!... And there couldn't possibly be such a fantastical creature as your Inquisitor. What are these sins of mankind they take upon themselves? Who are these keepers of the mystery who've taken on some curse for the sake of humanity's happiness? When has anyone ever seen such people? We know the Jesuits, people speak ill of them, but surely they're not really what you've described? They're nothing like that, nothing at all.... They're simply the Roman army, working toward earthly dominion over the world in the future, with the Pontiff of Rome as Emperor... that's their ideal, but there's no mystery in it, no lofty melancholy whatsoever.... It's plain lust for power, for filthy earthly gain, for domination—something like universal serfdom, with them as the masters—that's all they stand for. They probably don't even believe in God. Your suffering Inquisitor is pure fantasy."

"Wait, wait," Ivan laughed, "how worked up you are! Fantasy, you say—fine, let it be so! Of course it's a fantasy. But let me ask you this: do you really think that the Roman Catholic movement, over these last centuries, is truly nothing but a lust for power, for filthy earthly gain? Is that what Father Païssy teaches?"

"No, no, quite the opposite, Father Païssy did once say something rather similar to what you're saying... but of course it's not really the same, not remotely the same," Alyosha corrected himself quickly.

"A telling admission, despite your 'not remotely the same.' Let me ask you—why do you assume your Jesuits and Inquisitors have banded together for nothing but vile material gain? Why couldn't there be, among them, even one martyr, weighed down by great sorrow and genuine love for mankind? Just suppose, for a moment, that among all those who supposedly crave nothing but filthy material gain, there was even one such man—one like my old Inquisitor, who himself lived on roots in the desert, who made frantic efforts to subdue his own flesh in order to make himself free and whole. And yet all his life he loved mankind, and then suddenly his eyes were opened, and he saw that there's no great moral blessing in achieving perfection and freedom, if along with it comes the conviction that millions of God's creatures were made as nothing but a mockery, that they'll never be capable of using their freedom, that these poor rebels can never grow into giants able to finish the tower, that it was never for such geese that the great idealist dreamed his dream of harmony. Seeing all this, he turned back and joined—the clever people. Surely something like that could have happened?"

"Joined whom, what clever people?" Alyosha cried, completely swept up now. "They have no such great cleverness, no mysteries, no secrets.... Maybe nothing but atheism, that's their whole secret. Your Inquisitor doesn't believe in God, that's his secret!"

"What if that's exactly it! At last you've guessed it. It's perfectly true, it's true that's the whole secret—but isn't that itself a kind of suffering, at least for a man like that, a man who wasted his entire life in the desert and still couldn't shake off his incurable love for humanity? In his old age he arrived at the clear conviction that nothing but the counsel of the great, dread spirit could ever build any tolerable kind of life for these feeble, unruly, 'incomplete, botched creatures created in jest.' And so, convinced of this, he understands that he has no choice but to follow the counsel of the wise spirit, the dread spirit of death and destruction, and therefore to accept lying and deception, and to lead men, quite consciously, toward death and destruction, all while deceiving them the entire way so they never notice where they're being led, so that these poor, blind creatures might at least believe themselves happy along the way. And notice—the deception is carried out in the name of the very one whose ideal the old man had believed in so fervently his whole life long. Isn't that tragic? And if even one such man stood at the head of that entire army, that army supposedly 'driven by nothing but the lust for power and filthy gain'—wouldn't just one such man be enough to create a tragedy? More than that—one such man at the head is enough to give rise to the actual guiding idea of the Roman Church, with its whole army of Jesuits, its highest idea. I'll tell you frankly, I firmly believe that there has always been at least one such man among those who've stood at the head of that movement. Who knows, there may even have been such a man among the Roman Popes themselves. Who knows, maybe the spirit of that cursed old man, who loves mankind so stubbornly, in his own strange way, can be found even now among a whole multitude of such old men, existing not by chance but by mutual agreement, as a secret league formed long ago to guard the mystery—to guard it from the weak and the unhappy, so as to make them happy. No doubt that's how it is, and how it has to be. I suspect even among the Freemasons there's something of that same mystery lurking at the bottom of it, and that's exactly why the Catholics despise the Masons so much, as rivals breaking apart the unity of the idea, when what's truly essential is that there be one flock and one shepherd.... But listen to how I'm defending my own idea—I sound like an author who can't stand criticism. Enough of that."

"Maybe you're a Freemason yourself!" burst suddenly from Alyosha. "You don't believe in God," he added, speaking this time with real sorrow. He suspected, too, that his brother was looking at him with irony. "How does your poem end?" he asked, suddenly looking down. "Or was that the end?"

"I meant to end it like this. When the Inquisitor stopped speaking, he waited a while for his Prisoner to answer him. His silence weighed on him. He saw that the Prisoner had listened intently the whole time, looking gently into his face, clearly with no wish to reply. The old man longed for Him to say something, however bitter, however terrible. But instead, He suddenly approached the old man in silence and softly kissed him on his bloodless, aged lips. That was His entire answer. The old man shuddered. His lips trembled. He walked to the door, opened it, and said to Him: 'Go, and do not come back... don't come at all, never, never!' And he let Him out into the dark alleys of the town. The Prisoner went away."
"And the old man?"
"The kiss burns on in his heart, but the old man holds fast to his idea."
"And you, along with him—you too?" Alyosha cried, sorrowfully.
Ivan laughed.

"Why, it's all nonsense, Alyosha. It's nothing but a senseless poem, written by a senseless student who could never write two lines of real verse. Why are you taking it so seriously? Surely you don't imagine I'm about to go running off to the Jesuits, to join the men correcting His work? Good Lord, it's none of my business. I told you, all I want is to make it to thirty, and then... dash the cup to the ground!"

"But the sticky little leaves, and the precious graves, and the blue sky, and the woman you love! How will you live, how will you love any of it?" Alyosha cried, sorrowfully. "With a hell like that in your heart, in your head, how can you? No, that's exactly why you're leaving—to go join them... and if you don't, you'll destroy yourself, you won't be able to bear it!"
"There's a strength that can endure anything," Ivan said, with a cold smile.
"What strength?"
"The strength of the Karamazovs—the strength of Karamazov baseness."
"You mean sinking into debauchery, smothering your soul in corruption?"
"Possibly even that... only perhaps I'll manage to avoid it until I'm thirty, and then—"
"How will you avoid it? By what means will you avoid it? That's impossible, given your ideas."
"In the Karamazov way, again."
"'Everything is permitted,' you mean? Everything is permitted, is that it?"
Ivan scowled, and suddenly turned strangely pale.

"Ah, you've picked up yesterday's phrase, the one that offended Miüsov so much—and that Dmitri pounced on so naively and paraphrased!" he smiled oddly. "Yes, if you like, 'everything is permitted,' since the words have already been spoken. I won't deny it. And Mitya's version isn't bad either."
Alyosha looked at him in silence.

"I thought that as I left here, I'd at least have you," Ivan said suddenly, with unexpected feeling; "but now I see that there's no place for me even in your heart, my dear little hermit. I won't renounce the formula 'everything is permitted'—will you renounce me over it, then, yes?"
Alyosha got up, went over to him, and softly kissed him on the lips.
"That's plagiarism," Ivan cried, thoroughly delighted. "You stole that straight out of my poem. Thank you all the same, though. Get up, Alyosha, it's time we were both going."
They went outside, but stopped at the entrance to the restaurant.

"Listen, Alyosha," Ivan began in a resolute voice, "if I really am able to love the sticky little leaves, it will only be because I remember you. It's enough for me that you're somewhere out there, and I won't lose my desire to live just yet. Is that enough for you? Take it as a declaration of love, if you like. And now you go right, and I'll go left. And that's enough, do you hear me, enough. I mean, even if I don't leave tomorrow—though I'm almost certain I will—and we meet again, don't say another word about any of this. I'm asking that of you specifically. And about Dmitri too, I'm asking you in particular, never bring him up to me again," he added, with sudden irritation. "It's all exhausted, it's all been said a hundred times over already, hasn't it? And I'll make you one promise in return. When I turn thirty and want to 'dash the cup to the ground,' wherever I happen to be, I'll come find you for one more talk, even if it means coming from America—you can count on that. I'll come on purpose. It'll be quite interesting to see what you've become by then. It's rather a solemn promise, you understand. And we really might be parting ways for seven years, or ten. Go on now, go to your Pater Seraphicus, he's dying. If he dies without you there, you'll be angry with me for keeping you. Goodbye, kiss me once more; that's it, now go."

Ivan turned suddenly and walked off without looking back. It was exactly the way Dmitri had left Alyosha the day before, though the two partings couldn't have been more different. The strange resemblance flashed like an arrow through Alyosha's mind, amid the distress and dejection of that moment. He waited there a moment, watching his brother go. He noticed, suddenly, that Ivan swayed slightly as he walked, and that his right shoulder seemed lower than his left. He'd never noticed that before. But all at once he too turned and almost ran toward the monastery. It was nearly dark, and he felt something close to fear; something new was rising up in him that he couldn't quite account for. The wind had picked up again, just as it had the evening before, and the ancient pines murmured gloomily around him as he entered the hermitage grove. He almost ran the whole way. "Pater Seraphicus—he got that name from somewhere—where from?" Alyosha wondered. "Ivan, poor Ivan, and when will I see you again?... Here's the hermitage. Yes, yes, that's who he is, Pater Seraphicus, he will save me—from him, and forever!"

Several times afterward he wondered how he could have so completely forgotten his brother Dmitri, the moment he left Ivan—when that very morning, only a few hours earlier, he'd resolved so firmly to find him and not give up the search, even if it meant not making it back to the monastery that night.
